articles.title: Could Bryce Young really be an MVP contender? Through 4 games, the numbers say yes
articles.summary: (AP) — After Bryce Young rifled a 9-yard pass to Darren Waller on fourth-and-4 in the fourth quarter Sunday night during what became Carolina’s sixth straigh...
articles.body:
CHARLOTTE, N.C. (AP) — After Bryce Young rifled a 9-yard pass to Darren Waller on fourth-and-4 in the fourth quarter Sunday night during what became Carolina's sixth straight scoring drive, the chants cascaded down from the upper deck at Bank of America Stadium.

Young finished off the Panthers' 32-26 win over the Detroit Lions with yet another impressive stat line. He completed 29 of 41 passes for 329 yards and two touchdowns while playing without two of his top three receivers.

Granted, it came against the league's worst pass defense .

But the idea of Young, who was benched two games into his second season in 2024, being an MVP candidate may not be far-fetched.

Through four games, the numbers put him among the league's best quarterbacks.

Ahead of Monday night's Falcons-Saints game, Young led the NFL in yards passing (1,268), passing first downs (63), completions of 10-plus yards (55), completions of 25-plus yards (13) and deep passing yards (321), and was tied for third in touchdown passes (nine).

He's on pace to throw for 5,389 yards and 38 touchdowns, which would shatter franchise records.

Young has thrown for at least 287 yards in all four games, a huge leap for a player who struggled to eclipse 175 yards passing for the better part of his first two seasons.

Now in his fourth season and third in the same offense, he is looking comfortable and confident.

If Young took any satisfaction from hearing those chants, he wasn't about to let on. The 5-foot-10 Young may lack size, but he's never been short on humility.

"Obviously the support is a huge blessing. I'm super grateful for this community, for the fan base," Young said. "But again, it doesn't affect us as a football team. It doesn't give us any extra yards, any extra points. We have to earn those."

Behind a strong run-pass option game, the Panthers were finally able to get Chuba Hubbard going.

Hubbard ran for 122 yards on 20 carries with two touchdowns , and he helped open up passing opportunities for Young. It was the first time this season the Panthers were able to use the run game to set up the pass.

"It was great to have a little bit of balance there with some of the RPOs and playing off the runs," coach Dave Canales said. "As you know, we're trying to get our run game going and we saw that happen (Sunday). The RPO loosens it up a little bit and allows you to have some optionality. You can start to dictate to the defense whether they can play zone or man and how they try to attack those things."

The run game has the potential to take another step forward once the Panthers get their starting offensive tackles back.

Ickey Ekwonu (knee) and Taylor Moton (lung clots) have yet to play this season. Moton could return after the bye this week, but Ekwonu remains at least a few more weeks away.

The Panthers need to find some answers at cornerback, which could mean bringing in help from outside the organization.

Carolina placed starting cornerbacks Jaycee Horn and Mike Jackson on injured reserve last week. Both are expected to miss about eight weeks.

Rookie Will Lee III and Akayleb Evans filled in Sunday night, but both struggled. Jared Goff threw for 412 yards and the Lions piled up 452 yards on offense.

With Jalen Coker (quadriceps) and Xavier Legette (knee) sidelined with injuries, Young leaned heavily on Tetairoa McMillan against the Lions, and last year's AP NFL Offensive Rookie of the Year didn't disappoint.

McMillan turned in one of the best single-game performances in franchise history with 14 catches for 192 yards and two touchdowns. He nearly broke Christian McCaffrey's team record of 15 catches and Steve Smith Sr.'s mark of 201 yards receiving after a week of practices in which he and Young struggled to connect.

"Everything was clicking for us tonight, and that's all you can ask for," McMillan said.

McMillan gave a shoutout to Smith after he scored his second touchdown, yelling into a television camera.

"Yeah, I ain't gonna lie, I don't know why I thought the camera had a mic," McMillan said. "So, I don't know why they didn't catch what I said. But I said, 'Shoutout to Steve Smith. If you see this face, that means I scored again.' So, I did a little tribute to him for sure."

Ryan Fitzgerald missed two extra points against the Lions.

Canales and the Panthers are happy to have an early bye this season.

Rookie offensive tackle Monroe Freeling (knee), the team's first-round draft pick, and outside linebacker Jaelan Phillips (hamstring) were injured against the Lions, but Canales said Monday that he is optimistic neither will miss any playing time.

The week off should give Coker and guard Damien Lewis (elbow) a chance to return in Week 6.

Canales also said the Panthers are close to getting running back Trevor Etienne and Moton back from injured reserve.

The Panthers have allowed three touchdown passes to opposing tight ends over the last two games.

The defending NFC South champion Panthers (2-2) head into the bye atop the division standings. They will be joined by the winner of the Falcons-Saints game. Carolina's next game is at Philadelphia on Oct. 18.

articles.title: Chargers' Khalil Mack receives major trade update after 0-4 start
articles.summary: The Chargers could move on from Khalil Mack if their season continues to unravel.
articles.body:
The Chargers season has unraveled in a big way.

They sit at 0-4 with no juice or momentum, as it's been a season from hell for Los Angeles. Nothing has gone right for the Chargers, and if that continues, Los Angeles may get calls about edge rusher Khalil Mack's availability.

ESPN NFL insider Adam Schefter says if the Chargers don't turn things around, Mack will be a hot commodity around the league.

"…Last year of his contract on a team that is not winning," Schefter said . "The Chargers need to turn it around to keep him. If not, they'll be getting calls about his availability."

Mack, 35, is playing on a one-year deal worth $18 million. There's also a chance that this could be Mack's final playing season.

The future Hall of Famer mulled over retiring this past offseason and has said he wants to make a deep playoff run and win a Super Bowl. As things stand, the Chargers are far from that.

If Los Angeles keeps going down this road, the Chargers should look for a new home for Mack.

The Chargers are in danger of going 0-5 as they will host their division rivals in Week 5, the Denver Broncos .

Mack's days as a Charger may be numbered.

articles.title: Joe Mixon Signs With The Seahawks, Impacting Emanuel Wilson's Fantasy Football Value
articles.summary: The Seattle Seahawks have signed veteran running back Joe Mixon.
articles.body:
With first-round pick Jadarian Price landing on injured reserve, the Seattle Seahawks have signed running back Joe Mixon. Mixon has been a fantasy superstar in the past, but missed all of 2025 while recovering from a foot injury. It looked like his career could be over, but he will attempt to make a comeback and return to fantasy relevance with the defending Super Bowl champions.

It's unclear when Mixon will get on the field or what his role will be. He will likely form some sort of committee with Emanuel Wilson and George Holani. Wilson was the clear lead back in Seattle in Week 4.

We know how great Mixon can be, but we don't know what we are going to get from him at 30 years old, coming off a serious foot injury. It's also not clear where he will land in the pecking order of the Seahawks backfield.

Mixon is worth a waiver wire add, but you shouldn't bank on him contributing to your team. He should be viewed as a speculative stash with the hopes that he looks close to his former self. Even if it takes him a while to become acclimated to the system and see more touches, it shouldn't take all that long to figure out if he still has it from an athletic perspective.

If we were to give our best guess, he would likely slide into a role similar to what we saw from Price. Once he gets rolling, we would expect him to see about eight carries and three targets per game, give or take.

Wilson was set to be one of, if not the top waiver wire targets on the week. The addition of Mixon kind of throws cold water on that. That's not to say he can't still be the lead back in Seattle, but those 21 carries and four targets we saw in Week 4 are now much less likely to be a sign of things to come.

His volume is now much more likely to land around 12 carries per game with a few targets. We might still get one more huge volume week out of him in Week 5, but his touches will likely be scaled back after that.

This addition of Mixon saps just about any interest fantasy owners could have had in Holani. Both his floor and upside are limited. At best, he could be a desperation flex. There is no need to pick him up off the waiver wire at this point.

articles.title: Bears offense among NFL’s best despite red zone issues
articles.summary: The Bears got a good game on both sides of the ball for the second consecutive week. @gridironborn and @wiltfongjr break it down here.
articles.body:
That's three weeks in a row the Chicago Bears have stumbled in the red zone, and it's something head coach Ben Johnson recognized and addressed in his opening remarks at his postgame press conference before he even fielded any questions about their win over the New York Jets.

"Obviously, we got to get better in the red zone," he said. "It's been really three weeks in a row that we've left points out there. So that'll be a major emphasis for us going forward, as well as the turnovers. We can't have those on offense, but overall, like I said, great job finding a way to get to three and one."

The Bears gave the ball away twice, once on a Tyson Bagent interception, and once on a D'Andre Swift fumble. Swift seemed to be sidelined after that, and I'd imagine Bagent's film session will be ugly, because he had a couple of other poor decisions. But all in all, it was a solid performance for Chicago's number two QB.

The Bears have one of the best offenses in the NFL, and each week they've made mistakes that cost them points. Whether that be penalties, execution, or bad play calls, they need to self-scout, clean some stuff up, and take the offense to the next level.

articles.title: Jets vs. Bears: What went right, what went wrong in Week 4
articles.summary: Breakdown of Jets vs. Bears: What went right, what went wrong in Week 4 loss.
articles.body:
The New York Jets entered Soldier Field hoping to even their record at 2-2, but they never found a way to establish control. The Chicago Bears dominated time of possession, repeatedly extended drives, and left the Jets with almost no opportunity to develop any offensive rhythm in a 23-12 win over the visitors .

The numbers tell just how one-sided the afternoon became. Chicago ran 89 offensive plays to New York's 32, held the football for 44:12 and limited the Jets to just 17:15 of possession. New York's 32 offensive plays were the second-fewest by a team in a game in NFL history, trailing only the expansion Cleveland Browns' 28-play performance against the Pittsburgh Steelers in 1999.

There were still a few positives worth carrying into Week 5, but they were buried underneath one of the Jets' most difficult performances of the season.

Minkah Fitzpatrick finally ended the interception drought. After more than 20 games and 83 quarters without an interception, the Jets finally got one when Fitzpatrick picked off Tyson Bagent. The timing was especially fitting because Fitzpatrick was returning from the groin injury that had sidelined him since Week 1, and he had acknowledged before the game that ending the drought would be "very nice" and "very sweet." Unfortunately, New York had three other apparent interceptions wiped away by penalties, making Fitzpatrick's play the only one that ultimately counted.

Demario Davis continues to show why his presence matters. Davis remained one of the Jets' most active defenders, flying toward the football and providing a steadying presence while Chicago controlled so much of the game. His production and energy continue to stand out, particularly for a defense that has asked its veterans to maintain their composure through some exhausting stretches.

Jamien Sherwood created another takeaway. Sherwood forced D'Andre Swift to fumble on a tackle, and Brandon Stephens recovered for New York's second successful takeaway of the afternoon. It was another encouraging sign for a defense that has consistently shown an ability to create disruption, even if it has not always been able to turn those opportunities into enough points.

Isaiah Williams provided one of the few offensive highlights. Williams scored the first receiving touchdown of his career, giving the Jets a badly needed jolt after the offense had spent much of the afternoon struggling to stay on the field. The play was a reminder that Williams can provide value beyond the return game, where he has already demonstrated big-play ability.

Round 1 went to Ben Johnson. The former Detroit Lions assistants entered the game knowing each other's philosophies well, and Johnson's offense won the opening exchange decisively. Chicago used pre-snap motion and repeatedly attacked the Jets with in-breaking routes over the middle, while Bagent completed five of six throws for 62 yards on the opening drive. The Bears looked prepared to attack exactly where Glenn's defense did not want to be tested.

The Jets couldn't stay on the field. New York ran just four plays in the first quarter while Chicago held the ball for 12:49 of the opening 15 minutes. By halftime, the Bears had run 49 plays and outgained the Jets 274-34, with Chicago also holding a 112-29 advantage on the ground. Geno Smith was 3-of-8 for 18 yards at the break, leaving the offense almost no chance to establish any rhythm.

The pass rush disappeared at the worst possible time. David Bailey recorded zero pressures on 27 pass-rush snaps, Will McDonald had one on 24, and Joseph Ossai finished with none on 19. Braiden McGregor also had no pressure before leaving with a chest injury. Harrison Phillips was the only Jets player to record more than one pressure, making it extremely difficult for the defense to consistently disrupt Chicago's passing game.

The Jets' interception drought ended, but the penalty problem made the accomplishment strangely complicated. New York recorded three interceptions that were wiped away by penalties. Ending the drought was significant, but the sequence also reinforced how often the Jets have made good plays and then found ways to undermine themselves.

The offense never got enough opportunities to recover. The Jets finished with only 32 offensive plays, meaning Smith and the rest of the unit spent much of the afternoon watching from the sideline. That does not excuse an offensive performance this poor, but it does explain why New York struggled to build any sustained momentum or rhythm. When one team runs nearly three times as many plays as the other, it becomes extremely difficult to dictate the terms of the game.

The numbers were historically ugly. Chicago's 89 offensive plays were 57 more than New York's, a disparity that ranks among the largest in NFL history. ESPN's Rich Cimini reports the Bears' 44:12 time of possession was their most in a game since 1994, while the Jets' 17:15 marked their lowest total time of possession since 2005. Those numbers aren't merely bad; they explain almost everything about how this game unfolded.

This wasn't another competitive loss that came down to a handful of late plays. The Bears controlled the game from the opening possession, and the Jets did not establish enough offensive rhythm to change that reality. The two takeaways and Fitzpatrick's long-awaited interception provided some encouragement, but they were overwhelmed by the sheer imbalance in opportunity.

The Jets have shown through the first four weeks that they can compete with talented teams when their defense, offense, and special teams complement one another. Sunday was the opposite. Chicago controlled the football, dictated the matchup, and forced New York to spend most of the afternoon reacting.

The Jets finally return home in Week 5 after playing three road games in their first four weeks, giving them an opportunity to reset against the Cleveland Browns . New York has plenty to correct before then, but the biggest priority should be finding a way to keep all three phases functioning together rather than asking one unit to overcome the shortcomings of another.

The Bears made the Jets look overwhelmed on Sunday . The response in Week 5 will tell us much more about whether that was an isolated collapse or a sign of deeper problems, because the Jets now have to show they can respond to adversity instead of allowing one ugly afternoon to become a turning point in the wrong direction.
